title: Highland Stand town-builder mini game: historical ground for one town in three ages
scope_note: Research only. Nothing here is game text until a writer turns it into short lines under the owner's text rules. Confidence: high = primary text or several solid secondary sources agree; moderate = one good secondary source or a dated tradition; low = thin or unsourced.
access_note: Wikipedia, Iranica, Britannica, UNESCO, Livius and all scholarly hosts were blocked (curl and WebFetch). I read: the offline Wikipedia snapshot; 66 further English Wikipedia articles (2023-06-01) from the TFDS mirror; Armenian Wikipedia hits; Perseus primary texts from GitHub (Tacitus, Strabo, Plutarch, Josephus, Suetonius, Ammianus); Lynch vol. 1; the campaign's own vetted docs. Six WebSearch calls were used; their summaries are marked WS and were not opened.

setting.recommendation: One town of the Ararat plain (the province of Ayrarat) through three ages: Erebuni (Urartian hill fort, 782 BC) to Artashat (classical capital, 176 BC; wonder window AD 66 to 77) to Dvin (early medieval capital; wonder window 640s to 650s). Wonders: the temple of Haldi at Erebuni, the temple of Garni, and Zvartnots.
setting.framing_for_players: The game's town is a composite. It stands for the royal seat of the Ararat plain, which moved as capitals rose and fell, all within sight of Mount Ararat. Say so once, plainly, in the intro.

why.claim: One plain, one horizon: Ararat to the south, Aragats to the north, the Araxes and its tributaries; the same grain and vines in every age.

sources.quote: In the north, the plain borders on Mount Aragats, and Mount Ararat in the south.

why.claim: Each age's town really was the leading seat of its time on this plain: the Arsacid 'Ayrarat' was the royal domain of the Ararat plain, and most capitals of Armenia lay in Ayrarat.

sources.quote: Most of the historical capitals of Armenia were located in this province, including Armavir, Yervandashat, Artashat, Vagharshapat, Dvin, Bagaran, Shirakavan, Kars and Ani
During the Arsacid period, Ayrarat referred to, in its narrowest sense, the royal domain consisting of the Ararat plain and its adjacent districts.

resources.food: Grain (wheat, barley, millet), vines and herds in every age. Age 1 adds beer and buried wine jars; Age 3 adds wine presses.
resources.wood: Scarce in every age (Armenia has few forests). Age 1 uses timber for roofs, columns and floors; Age 2 for palisades; Age 3 can draw on Khosrov's planted forests near Artashat and Dvin.
resources.stone: Plentiful: basalt and tuff. Age 1 basalt footings under mudbrick; Age 2 clamped basalt ashlar; Age 3 tuff faces on a lime-mortar core.
resources.gold: Age 1: trade goods and tribute (barter; never coins). Age 2: coin (Armenian coins from Orontid times; Artashat's mint and customs house). Age 3: trade through the merchants' quarter and the red dye.

license_flags: The one-town composite is game license; disclose it once.
Raid timing, raid size and raiders reaching the town's own walls (above all the Alans in Age 2) are game license.

A wonder finished under attack is license, but grounded: Zvartnots was really built during the first Arab raids; Garni rose in the decade of the Alan raid; Erebuni was founded in a year of war with Etiuni.
Each victory card should then say what really happened, as the campaign's victory texts do.
art_threads: Mount Ararat on the southern horizon and Aragats to the north in all three ages.
Age 1: mudbrick on basalt footings, buttresses, corner towers, rows of jar shoulders in the cellars, the painted temple with its tower and twelve-column portico.
Age 2: walls over a ring of hills, the river on three sides, a trench and palisade on the fourth, a bridge; at Garni an Ionic temple of gray basalt on a high podium.
Age 3: domed stone churches, a three-part city (citadel, shahastan, suburb), columned palace halls with wooden roofs, the round church of Zvartnots. No khachkars, no bell towers, no caravanserais.

ages.dateline: Erebuni, Kingdom of Urartu (Biainili), 8th century BC (founded 782 BC by the usual dating)
ages.town: Erebuni, on the hill of Arin Berd at the southeastern edge of today's Yerevan. Teishebaini (Karmir Blur), built about a century later on the Hrazdan, is the natural late-age extension.
ages.campaign_link: Same place and year as the campaign's first battlefield, Erebuni Rise (era 0, 782 BC), which already uses Argishti I, Haldi and 'Etiuni Raiders'.
ages.summary: Argishti I raised Erebuni in 782 BC, by the usual dating, on newly conquered land north of the Araxes. Its citadel held a palace with a columned hall, a temple of Haldi, garrison quarters and storerooms for grain, oil and wine. A town of houses lay at the foot of the hill. Canals watered the plain. In the next century Rusa II built Teishebaini nearby, and Erebuni lost its place. No siege of Erebuni is recorded; late in Urartian times it seems to have been left without a fight.

core_claims.claim: Argishti I founded Erebuni in 782 BC on Arin Berd as a stronghold for the kingdom's northern border.

sources.quote: It was built on top of a hill called Arin Berd overlooking the Aras River Valley to serve as a military stronghold to protect the kingdom's northern borders.
Scholars date the start of his reign a little differently, so 782 BC is the usual date, not a certain one.

core_claims.note: This is the king's own claim. Handle with care in a family game: the settlers were captives.

core_claims.claim: Later kings used Erebuni as a base for campaigns to the north.

sources.quote: Kings Sarduri II and Rusa I also utilized Erebuni as a staging site for new campaigns of conquest directed towards the north.

core_claims.claim: Rusa II built Teishebaini (Karmir Blur) in the mid-7th century BC, and Erebuni lost its leading role.

safe_lines.text: Argishti I founded Erebuni in 782 BC, by the usual dating.
The kings of Urartu called their land Biainili.
Erebuni's storerooms held grain, oil and wine. Inscriptions at the doors told how much each held.
Great jars were sunk halfway into the ground to keep wine cool.
A painting in Erebuni's temple shows the god Haldi standing on a lion.
Urartian kings dug canals to water the Ararat plain.
Urartu traded by barter. It had no coins.
No siege of Erebuni is recorded. Late in Urartian times its garrison seems to have left it without a fight.
Teishebaini burned in a night attack early in the 6th century BC. Who the attackers were is still debated.

ages.dateline: Artashat (Artaxata), founded 176 BC by Artaxias I; the age's wonder window is AD 66 to 77, when the Arsacid king Tiridates I rebuilt the burned city and raised the temple at Garni
ages.town: Artashat on the Araxes, on nine hills at the meeting of the Araxes and the Metsamor, with its citadel on the hill now crowned by Khor Virap monastery. The royal fortress of Garni stands in the Azat gorge east of Yerevan, in the hills above the plain.
ages.campaign_link: No campaign battlefield covers this age. The campaign touches Artashat once: the council of 449 in the Avarayr chronicle. Dvin, the Age 3 town, was built just north of Artashat.
ages.summary: Artaxias I founded Artashat about 176 BC. Strabo saw a royal city guarded by the river on all sides but one, where a trench and palisade closed the neck of land. It had baths, markets, workshops, a treasury, a mint and a customs house. Roman legions under Corbulo took and burned it in AD 58 or 59. Tiridates I, crowned in Rome by Nero in 66, came home with craftsmen to rebuild it, and embellished the royal fortress at Garni with a new temple. Around 72 the Alans raided Armenia and nearly captured him.

ages.town: Dvin on the Metsamor, just north of old Artashat, about 35 km south of modern Yerevan. Zvartnots rose near Vagharshapat on the same plain; Nerses III also built a chapel at Khor Virap on Artashat's old citadel hill.

ages.summary: Tradition credits King Khosrov III with building Dvin around 335. After 428 it was the seat of the Persian-appointed marzpans, and by the 6th century of the catholicos. Procopius found merchants trading goods from India to Rome there. Its cathedral of St. Gregory became a domed church by the mid-7th century. In 640 an Arab raid took and sacked Dvin. In 643 Theodoros Rshtuni defeated a second Arab army, and Sebeos says an Arab army could not take the fortress of Erevan. In these same years Catholicos Nerses III the Builder raised the round church of Zvartnots, consecrated in 652.

wonder.name: Zvartnots Cathedral
wonder.builder: Catholicos Nerses III the Builder (Shinogh; catholicos 641 to 661)
wonder.date: Begun 643 (641 in Armenian sources); consecrated 652 according to Movses Kaghankatvatsi; work went on 653 to 659 under Anastas Akoratsi while Nerses was in Tayk. Fell in the 10th century.
wonder.location: Near Vagharshapat (Ejmiatsin), on the Ararat plain west of Yerevan
wonder.description: A round church: a 32-sided outer wall that looked circular, around a cross-shaped core with an aisle, rising in tiers to a dome (Toramanian's three-tier reconstruction of 1905 is widely accepted but disputed). Mosaics, eagle capitals, basket capitals and vine scrolls. Dedicated to St. Gregory, where tradition placed the meeting of King Trdat III and Gregory. The catholicos' palace and a winery stood beside it. UNESCO World Heritage since 2000.
wonder.confidence: high for builder and the 640s to 650s; moderate for the exact start year and the three-tier form

safe_lines.text: From a distance Zvartnots looked round. Its outer wall had 32 sides.

Sebeos wrote that an Arab army fought against the fortress of Erevan and could not take it.

alternatives_weighed.for: The strongest 'medieval city': Smbat II's double northern walls, Trdat's cathedral (989 to 1001 or 1010), a Zvartnots copy (Gagkashen, 1001 to 1005); raiders with dates (Byzantine claim 1041 to 1044; Seljuk siege of 25 days and sack, 1064).
alternatives_weighed.against: Ani is in Shirak on the Akhurian gorge (today in Turkey's Kars province), not on the Ararat plain. My sources show no Urartian or classical town there (its oldest walls are on the citadel, from the 7th-century Kamsarakan period), so the 'one town' idea breaks. Ani is already a full campaign battlefield (Ani, 1041) with this exact story. The 1064 sack ends in massacre, heavy for a family game. The Bagratid kingdom minted no coins of its own.
alternatives_weighed.verdict: Not recommended for Age 3. Possible later as an optional Age 4.
